items.name: Sell Mineral Rights in Weld County, CO
items.meta: Weld County is Colorado's top oil-producing county and the heart of the Wattenberg Field. Get a comp-based cash offer on your Niobrara or Codell interest.

sections.html:
Weld County produces more oil than any other county in Colorado, and it's the single most consistent market we work in for Niobrara and Codell mineral interests.

Weld County is the core of the Wattenberg Field and, by a wide margin, the largest oil-producing county in Colorado. Horizontal drilling into the Niobrara and Codell formations has run here continuously for more than a decade, laterals have stretched from one mile to two, three, and now sometimes four miles as operators consolidate acreage into fewer, larger pads. If you own minerals anywhere in Weld County, you're sitting in the state's most active and most closely watched oil and gas market, which is both an advantage and a reason to be precise about valuation.

That said, Weld County is a big place, and the difference between a tract in the deep Wattenberg core and one on the county's outer edge can be significant. Before we quote a number, we look at exactly where your section sits, what's currently producing around it, and what your division order actually shows.

sections.title: A county that stayed open after SB 19-181
sections.html:
When Colorado passed SB 19-181 in 2019, giving local governments direct authority over oil and gas siting and shifting the state's regulatory mission toward public health and environmental protection, many Front Range municipalities responded by tightening local setbacks and permitting review. Weld County took a different path, working to become one of the state's designated Local Government Designees, which lets the county run its own expedited local review for oil and gas permits under COGCC's statewide framework rather than defaulting to slower state-level review.

The practical effect is that Weld County has stayed one of the more predictable places in Colorado to permit a new well, even as some of its own edge communities, and plenty of neighboring Adams and Broomfield-area suburbs, have adopted more cautious postures. That relative predictability is part of why operators like Civitas Resources and Oxy have continued to concentrate their Colorado drilling budgets here rather than spreading them thinner across the Front Range.

sections.title: Who's operating in Weld County today
sections.html:
Civitas Resources, formed through the 2021 merger of Bonanza Creek, Extraction Oil & Gas, and Crestone Peak Resources and expanded further by its 2023 acquisition of PDC Energy, holds one of the largest positions in the Wattenberg Field. Occidental Petroleum, which inherited a major DJ Basin position through its 2019 acquisition of Anadarko, and Anadarko itself before that through Kerr-McGee's legacy Wattenberg holdings, is the other dominant operator across much of the county. Chevron also holds meaningful acreage.

Multi-well pad development is standard practice now, with operators drilling four, eight, sometimes more than a dozen wells from a single surface location to minimize surface disturbance and reach as many spacing units as possible from one pad. For a mineral owner, that means your specific tract's value increasingly depends on whether it falls inside a currently planned multi-well unit, not only whether oil and gas exists underneath it.

sections.title: Split estate and the county's agricultural roots
sections.html:
Weld County was homesteaded and farmed for irrigated corn, sugar beets, and wheat long before the Niobrara became a household name in oil and gas circles. Many mineral owners today hold interests that trace back to those original farm families, sometimes retained when the surface sold, sometimes passed down through several generations of heirs with no direct connection to the land itself anymore.

That history means title work is rarely simple. We routinely find Weld County interests with a dozen or more heirs on record, and no two chains of title look exactly alike.

sections.title: Forced pooling and small fractional owners
sections.html: Because so much Weld County mineral ownership is fractionalized across heirs, forced pooling orders from the COGCC are a routine part of how operators assemble a horizontal spacing unit. If your interest was pooled, your division order should list a specific decimal share tied to a defined unit, and we verify that share against the underlying pooling order and current production data before making an offer.

sections.title: What the Weld County Clerk and Recorder confirms
sections.html: Every offer starts with the record. We pull your chain of title directly from the Weld County Clerk and Recorder in Greeley, confirm the mineral reservation survived every subsequent transfer, cross-reference your division order and any active lease, and only then price your interest against recent, comparable Wattenberg transactions rather than a flat countywide number.

faqs.q: Why is Weld County treated as the benchmark for DJ Basin pricing?
faqs.a: It's the largest oil-producing county in the state and the deepest, most consistently developed part of the Wattenberg Field, so recent Weld County transactions are the most reliable comps we have for the broader DJ Basin.

faqs.q: Does it matter where in Weld County your tract sits?
faqs.a: Yes, significantly. Deep-core Wattenberg acreage prices differently than the county's outer flanks, so we always check your specific section before quoting a number.

faqs.q: you have a small fractional interest split among several heirs. Is it still worth selling?
faqs.a: Yes, we regularly buy small fractional interests. We confirm each heir's exact share through the county record and any applicable pooling order before making an offer.

faqs.q: How does SB 19-181 affect drilling in Weld County specifically?
faqs.a: Weld County pursued Local Government Designee status to keep permitting review local and relatively efficient, which has helped it stay more predictable for operators than some neighboring counties that adopted stricter local setbacks.

faqs.q: How quickly can a Weld County sale close?
faqs.a: Once we confirm your chain of title and current division order, most Weld County transactions close within two to four weeks.

items.name: Sell Mineral Rights in Garfield County, CO
items.meta: Own Piceance Basin gas minerals in Garfield County? We price interests from Rifle to Parachute off real decline data and close directly with owners.

sections.html:
Garfield County is the historical center of Piceance Basin gas development in Colorado, and mineral ownership here spans everything from decades-old vertical wells still paying modest royalties to large undeveloped tracts that have never been leased.

Piceance gas is fundamentally a different asset than the oil-driven DJ Basin production owners farther east are more used to hearing about. Wells in the Mamm Creek, Rulison, and Grand Valley fields around Rifle, Silt, New Castle, and Parachute produce primarily from the Mancos and Williams Fork formations, and development pace here has always tracked natural gas prices closely rather than following a steady, predictable schedule.

That gas-price sensitivity created real boom-and-slowdown cycles across the county: dense vertical and directional drilling through the mid-2000s, a long pullback as gas prices sat depressed for years, and periodic renewed permitting activity since, concentrated in areas where operators already hold established infrastructure. If your family has held Garfield County minerals for a while, there is a good chance the interest has seen at least one productive period, even if things look quiet right now.

We buy Garfield County mineral interests directly, whether they are currently producing, held by older production that has gone dormant, or entirely unleased ranch and agricultural ground. Pricing depends heavily on which of those three categories your tract falls into, and we walk through that with you before quoting anything.

sections.title: Mamm Creek, Rulison, and the eastern county fields
sections.html:
The dense drilling that built much of Garfield County's Piceance production history happened east of Glenwood Springs, around Silt and Rifle, where operators developed the Mamm Creek and Rulison fields with hundreds of wells through the 2000s boom. Interests in this area typically have long, well-documented production histories, which we price using a decline curve fit to your actual check stub data rather than a generic assumption for the basin.

Because so much has been drilled and sold in this corridor, we also have deep comparable sale data to check any decline-curve-based offer against, giving owners here more pricing confidence than in less-developed parts of the county.

sections.title: The western county and Grand Valley gas fields
sections.html: Farther west toward Parachute and the Grand Valley, similar Mancos and Williams Fork gas development has occurred, though with its own distinct permitting and infrastructure history separate from the Rifle-Silt corridor. We evaluate western county interests on their own production record rather than assuming they mirror the eastern fields.

sections.title: Undeveloped ranch and agricultural acreage
sections.html:
A meaningful share of Garfield County mineral ownership sits under ranch and farmland that has never been leased, or was leased during a past regional push without any well following. We price this speculative acreage against comparable regional lease and sale activity, and we are direct that these offers run lower than producing-interest offers, since there is no revenue stream to underwrite against.

Split estate is common throughout the county, meaning the surface owner and mineral owner are often different people. That does not change your right to lease or sell your mineral interest, but it does affect how quickly an operator can negotiate the surface access needed to actually drill, which we factor into how we time-adjust value on undeveloped acreage.

sections.title: Title work through Garfield County records
sections.html: We pull recorded leases, division orders, and unit agreements from the Garfield County Clerk and Recorder to confirm your exact net revenue interest. This step matters more here than in a newer basin, because Piceance assets have changed operators multiple times over the past two decades as larger companies sold mature holdings to smaller ones, and we want your paperwork to match current reality before finalizing an offer.

faqs.q: Why has drilling activity in Garfield County slowed down at various points?
faqs.a: Piceance wells are primarily gas plays, and gas prices have been softer than oil prices for extended stretches over the past decade, which slows new permitting even when existing wells keep producing.

faqs.q: Is an older, declined well in Garfield County still worth selling?
faqs.a: Often yes. We price the remaining production off your actual check stub trend using a decline curve, rather than assuming peak output has continued.

faqs.q: your royalty operator has changed names multiple times over the years. Is that a problem?
faqs.a: No, this is common across the Piceance Basin as assets have changed hands between operators. We confirm the current operator of record before finalizing any offer.

faqs.q: How is undeveloped Garfield County acreage priced differently than producing acreage?
faqs.a: Producing acreage is priced off a decline curve applied to real revenue. Undeveloped acreage is priced against comparable regional lease and sale activity, since there is no production history to underwrite against, and typically prices lower.

faqs.q: Does split estate ownership complicate a sale?
faqs.a: No, you can sell your mineral interest regardless of who owns the surface. Split estate mainly affects how quickly a future operator can negotiate surface access for new drilling, which we factor into how we value undeveloped acreage.

faqs.q: What documents speed up a Garfield County offer the most?
faqs.a: A division order and several months of recent check stubs for producing interests. For undeveloped acreage, a copy of your deed and any historical lease paperwork, even if expired, helps us price accurately.

items.name: Sell Mineral Rights in Mesa County, CO
items.meta: Own minerals in Mesa County, CO around Grand Junction and Palisade? We evaluate Piceance flank gas history and oil shale-era land records before quoting.

sections.html:
Mesa County sits on the western edge of the Piceance Basin, where the Grand Valley's orchard and vineyard country overlays a mineral history shaped as much by federal oil shale reserves as by conventional natural gas drilling.

Grand Junction, Palisade, Fruita, and the smaller communities around them make up a county with a genuinely mixed oil and gas story. Parts of Mesa County sit close enough to the Piceance Basin's productive core to have seen real gas development; other parts, particularly toward the Book Cliffs and the old Naval Oil Shale Reserve lands, carry a resource history that never converted into commercial oil shale production despite decades of federal and private interest.

Mineral ownership here often traces back to homestead-era agricultural patents — the Grand Valley's fruit orchards and vineyards sit on some of the oldest irrigated farmland in western Colorado, and the mineral rights beneath that ground were frequently severed and passed down separately from the surface as the valley's farm economy developed.

sections.title: Piceance flank geology versus Garfield County's core
sections.html:
Mesa County sits on the flank of the Piceance Basin rather than its productive core, which runs more heavily through Garfield County to the east around Rifle, Parachute, and the Mamm Creek and Rulison fields. Williams Fork and Mesaverde gas-bearing sands do extend into parts of Mesa County, but development density has always been lighter here, and much of the county's mineral acreage has never seen a well.

That flank position means valuing a Mesa County interest starts with a basic question: has anything actually been drilled and produced on this specific section, or is this undeveloped acreage carrying speculative rather than income-based value? We check Colorado Oil and Gas Conservation Commission records well by well rather than assuming either answer.

sections.title: The oil shale legacy and what it means for mineral owners
sections.html:
For much of the twentieth century, the Piceance Basin's oil shale deposits — concentrated in the Green River formation — drew heavy federal and private interest as a potential future energy source, including designated Naval Oil Shale Reserve lands partly within Mesa County. That interest peaked and collapsed more than once, most notably with Exxon's 1982 Black Sunday shutdown of its Colony oil shale project in neighboring Garfield County, and oil shale has never become commercially viable at scale in Colorado.

The practical legacy for mineral owners is mostly about land and title history rather than current production — some parcels carry old reservations, easements, or federal land exchange history connected to that oil shale era, which can occasionally complicate a title search. It doesn't mean oil shale-designated land has current oil and gas value; that still depends on actual drilling history.

sections.title: What we check before quoting a Mesa County interest
sections.html:
We start with your legal description and confirm whether any well has ever been permitted or has produced on that section through COGCC records. Where a well exists, we pull its production history and value the interest against actual paid volumes and decline stage. Where nothing has been drilled, we're direct that the interest reflects speculative potential, priced accordingly rather than inflated to match producing DJ Basin or core Piceance acreage.

Mesa County's clerk and recorder's office in Grand Junction holds the deed and lease history we need to trace ownership, particularly for older homestead-era mineral severances common throughout the Grand Valley.

sections.title: Fruit country title tracing
sections.html:
Orchard and vineyard families around Palisade, Orchard Mesa, and the Redlands often kept mineral rights separate as the same land changed hands between growers over multiple generations, sometimes without any oil and gas activity ever occurring to prompt a closer look at what was actually reserved. That means a fair number of Mesa County interests we evaluate haven't been actively managed in decades, and getting a current title picture is the first real step.

If your family's records are thin, we can help identify what to search for at the county clerk and recorder's office, whether that's an original homestead patent, a later deed reservation, or a probate filing tying the interest to your name today.

faqs.q: Is Mesa County part of the productive Piceance gas core?
faqs.a: It sits on the western flank rather than the core, which is concentrated further east in Garfield County. Some Mesa County sections have seen drilling; many haven't.

faqs.q: What is the Naval Oil Shale Reserve and does it affect your mineral rights?
faqs.a: It's a historic federal land designation tied to oil shale research that never became commercial production. It mainly affects title and land history rather than current oil and gas value.

faqs.q: How do you know if your Grand Valley property has ever been drilled?
faqs.a: We check COGCC well records against your legal description and tell you plainly whether there's any production history tied to your acreage.

faqs.q: Is undeveloped Mesa County acreage worth selling?
faqs.a: It can be, though the value reflects speculative long-term potential rather than a current royalty stream, and we price it with that distinction made clear.

items.name: Sell Mineral Rights in Rio Blanco County, CO
items.meta: Own minerals in Rio Blanco County, CO around Meeker or Rangely? We evaluate Piceance gas and the historic Rangely CO2-flood oil field before quoting.

sections.html:
Rio Blanco County holds two distinct resource stories under one roof: Piceance Basin natural gas in the county's east and south, and the historic, still-producing Rangely oil field along the Utah border to the west.

Meeker anchors the county's northern ranch country while Rangely sits over one of the largest oil fields ever discovered in Colorado, still producing today after nearly a century thanks to a long-running carbon dioxide enhanced recovery program. Between those two poles, Rio Blanco County mineral owners can be holding very different kinds of interests depending on where exactly their acreage sits, and the White River corridor running through much of the county has shaped both ranching history and oil and gas access for generations.

Mineral ownership across the county traces overwhelmingly to ranching and homestead families, with mineral rights kept separate from surface land as large cattle operations were bought, sold, and passed down through the decades.

sections.title: The Rangely field: enhanced recovery, not shale decline
sections.html:
Discovered in the 1930s and developed heavily through mid-century, the Rangely field has been sustained for decades by Chevron's CO2 injection program into the Weber sandstone reservoir, a very different production profile than the sharp-peak, fast-decline curves typical of modern shale plays. Most mineral interests tied to Rangely sit inside a long-established unit agreement, with royalties allocated by formula across the unit rather than a single well.

Valuing a Rangely-area interest means looking at the field's current recovery program status and unit allocation, not only historical output from decades ago, since the ongoing CO2 flood economics drive what the field produces today.

sections.title: Piceance Basin gas around Meeker and the county's eastern reach
sections.html:
The Williams Fork and Mesaverde formations that define Piceance Basin gas production extend into eastern and southern Rio Blanco County, though development density here has generally been lighter than the Garfield County core around Rifle and Parachute. Some Rio Blanco County acreage has seen real horizontal and vertical gas development; other sections remain undrilled ranch ground.

We check COGCC well and production records specific to each parcel we evaluate here, since assuming uniform development across a county this large and geologically varied would misstate the real picture for most owners.

sections.title: Ranch land, split estate, and title tracing
sections.html:
Because so much of the county has remained in large family ranch holdings, mineral severance here often happened cleanly within a family rather than through outside sale, though inheritance across multiple generations without formal probate can still complicate title. The Rio Blanco County clerk and recorder's office in Meeker holds the deed, lease, and unit records we use to trace ownership before quoting anything.

White River National Forest and BLM land also borders significant portions of the county, which can affect access and development feasibility on adjacent private mineral acreage even where the underlying mineral estate itself is privately held.

sections.title: What we ask for before quoting
sections.html:
Your deed or legal description is the starting point for any Rio Blanco County evaluation, and if the interest is tied to Rangely, we'll also ask whether you have a copy of the unit agreement or a recent division order showing your participation percentage. For Meeker-area acreage, prior lease documents help even without a well ever having been drilled, since they establish a documented history of interest in the ground.

Given the size of the county and the very different resource stories at its eastern and western ends, we treat every Rio Blanco County interest individually rather than pricing off a single countywide assumption.

faqs.q: What's the difference between Rangely and the rest of the county's oil and gas activity?
faqs.a: Rangely is a mature, unitized oil field sustained by decades of CO2 enhanced recovery, while the rest of the county's activity is mostly conventional Piceance Basin natural gas with a more typical decline pattern.

faqs.q: Is your mineral interest part of the Rangely unit or a separate well?

faqs.a: It can affect access and drilling feasibility on nearby private acreage, which is part of what we check when evaluating undeveloped interests in the county.

faqs.a: Some Rio Blanco County ranching families accumulated land or minerals in more than one part of the county across generations, sometimes through separate purchases or inheritances, which is why we always check each parcel independently rather than assuming a single unified interest.

faqs.a: Usually title clarity. A well-documented single-owner interest can close quickly, while one split across several heirs or tied to older, less-organized records takes longer to confirm before we can finalize a purchase.

items.name: Sell Mineral Rights in Rangely, CO
items.meta: Own minerals near Rangely, CO's historic oil field? We check the long-producing White River field's CO2-flood history before quoting your interest.

sections.html:
Rangely sits on top of one of Colorado's largest and longest-producing oil fields, discovered in the 1930s and still yielding oil today thanks to decades of enhanced recovery work.

The Rangely oil field is a different animal from the shale-driven Niobrara and Piceance gas plays elsewhere in the state. Chevron has operated a long-running carbon dioxide flood here since the 1980s, injecting CO2 to push additional oil out of the Weber sandstone reservoir long after primary production would have otherwise tapered off. If your family held mineral rights around Rangely, there's a good chance they've been collecting royalties, in some form, for two, three, or more generations.

sections.title: Why enhanced recovery changes the value conversation
sections.html:
A CO2-flood field behaves very differently than a typical shale decline curve. Rather than a sharp early peak followed by rapid decline, enhanced recovery projects can sustain meaningful production for decades, with output tied to ongoing injection economics rather than the original reservoir pressure alone. That means valuing a Rangely interest requires looking at the field's current recovery program status, not only historical production averages.

Because the field has been under unitized development for so long, most Rangely-area mineral interests sit inside an established unit agreement rather than an individual well-by-well lease, which is worth understanding clearly before any sale.

faqs.q: What does it mean that your mineral interest is unitized?
faqs.a: It means your royalty is allocated based on a formula covering the whole field unit rather than tied to one specific well, which is standard for a field under enhanced recovery like Rangely.

faqs.q: How does CO2 flood production affect your royalty payments?

sections.html:
La Plata County sits over one of the most productive coalbed methane fields in the country, where the Fruitland coal formation has been giving up gas for more than three decades.

La Plata County, led by the county seat of Durango and the smaller town of Bayfield, is the Colorado heart of the San Juan Basin — a basin that straddles the Colorado-New Mexico line and has produced coalbed methane out of the Fruitland formation since the industry figured out how to dewater and drain those coal seams in the 1980s and 1990s. If you hold minerals here, they're most likely tied to a well that's been producing, at some level, for twenty or thirty years.

Mineral ownership in La Plata County runs deep and fractional. Original homestead and ranch patents from the early 1900s split minerals off from surface repeatedly as land passed through families, and by now it's common for a single well's spacing unit to have dozens of owners, each holding a small piece.

sections.title: How Fruitland coal CBM production actually behaves
sections.html:
Coalbed methane wells don't behave like a shale horizontal. Early on, operators pump water off the coal seam to drop pressure and let gas desorb, so early production can look modest while water volumes are high. Once a well matures, gas output typically settles into a long, gently declining tail that can run for decades — very different from the sharp early-peak, fast-decline curve you'd see in a Niobrara well up in the DJ Basin.

That long-tail behavior is actually useful when we value an interest: a well with fifteen or twenty years of recorded history gives us a real decline trend to extrapolate from, rather than a projection built on a few months of early data. We pull that production history from Colorado Oil and Gas Conservation Commission records well by well.

Some La Plata County wells have also gone through refracturing or recompletion work over the years as operators tried to access untapped coal intervals. That can reset or bump a decline curve, which is exactly the kind of detail that changes a valuation and that we check for before quoting.

sections.title: Split estate and fractional ownership realities
sections.html:
Split estate is the norm here, not the exception. Surface ranches around Bayfield and the Animas Valley have often changed hands multiple times while the minerals stayed with descendants of the original patent holder, sometimes divided across a dozen heirs after multiple generations of inheritance without a will. If you're holding a 1/64th interest or smaller from a family situation like that, you're not unusual for this county.

The La Plata County clerk and recorder's office in Durango holds the lease, deed, and pooling order filings we need to trace an interest back to its origin, and because this is one of the older-developed basins in the state, that paper trail can run long. We do that legwork before we ever put a number in front of you.

sections.title: Forced pooling and unit participation
sections.html:
Colorado's forced pooling framework means that if you own a fractional interest inside a spacing unit and haven't leased, an operator can still bring your interest into the unit under a compulsory pooling order, typically at a statutory royalty rate unless you've negotiated otherwise. That's common in older San Juan Basin units where original leases lapsed or were never signed by every heir.

If your interest is currently pooled rather than under a private lease, that changes both what you're owed and what a buyer will pay, since pooled interests carry a defined statutory royalty rather than a negotiated one. We check pooling status as part of every La Plata County evaluation.

faqs.q: What formation produces gas in La Plata County?

sections.html:
Las Animas County, led by Trinidad, sits over the Colorado portion of the Raton Basin, where coalbed methane wells drilled through the Vermejo and Raton formation coals have produced steadily since the 1990s boom.

Las Animas County's mineral history runs deeper than most people realize — coal mining shaped Trinidad and the surrounding towns for a century before coalbed methane development arrived and started producing gas from those same coal seams, this time without anyone going underground. If your family held land near Trinidad, Kim, Segundo, or Lynn, there's a real chance your minerals sit over a CBM well that's been paying, at some level, for twenty-plus years.

sections.title: How Raton Basin CBM wells produce and decline
sections.html:

That's a very different curve from the steep early peak and fast decline of a Niobrara horizontal up in the DJ Basin, and it means older Las Animas County wells often have twenty or more years of usable production history to value against.

Some wells drilled during the initial 1990s boom have since been recompleted or had additional coal intervals accessed, which can extend or reshape the decline curve. We check well-specific COGCC production data rather than assuming every CBM well in the county behaves identically.

sections.title: Produced water handling and its effect on economics
sections.html:
Raton Basin CBM development historically generated significant produced water volumes that operators had to manage — through disposal wells, treatment, or surface discharge under permit. Water handling costs are part of why some marginal CBM wells have been shut in or plugged over the years even while gas prices held reasonably steady, and it's a factor in why not every legacy interest in the county still has an active producing well behind it.

If your interest is tied to a well that's been shut in, that doesn't necessarily mean it's worthless — some wells get returned to production, and the lease itself may still hold value depending on its terms — but it does change how we approach the valuation.

sections.title: Legacy operators and ownership changes

The Las Animas County clerk and recorder's office in Trinidad holds the deed, lease, and pooling records we use to confirm your interest's history and current standing, and because this basin has been developed for decades, that record can run long.

items.name: Sell Mineral Rights in Adams County, CO
items.meta: Own DJ Basin minerals in Adams County? See how Wattenberg-adjacent production, urban setbacks, and county records shape what buyers pay before you sell.

sections.html:
Adams County sits on the northeast flank of Denver's suburban expansion and directly over the northern reach of the Wattenberg Field, which puts a growing share of its mineral acreage inside the collision between horizontal Niobrara development and residential growth.

Adams County minerals get valued differently depending on which side of that collision they sit on. Acreage near Brighton, Commerce City, and the Weld County line has seen active horizontal pads targeting the Niobrara and Codell benches of the DJ Basin, with production runs that show up on a division order the way any Wattenberg well would. Acreage further south and west, closer to built-out Denver suburbs, is more likely to be held by older vertical wells or leases that never got developed once the surface use conflicts hardened.

We buy and evaluate Adams County mineral and royalty interests county-wide, but we underwrite the two situations differently. A producing interest gets priced off decline curves and recent check stubs. An undeveloped or stale lease gets priced off what's actually permittable given today's setback rules, not what a landman might have quoted in 2014.

sections.title: Where the county sits in the DJ Basin
sections.html:
The productive core of the Wattenberg Field is centered in Weld County, but Adams County catches the northern and western edges of that same Niobrara-Codell stack. Operators drilling multi-well pads along the Adams-Weld line have extended laterals that cross county boundaries, which means a mineral tract can be pooled into a unit that's mostly in one county and partly in the other. If your family's minerals were assigned by legal description decades ago, it's worth checking whether a modern horizontal unit even lines up with those original boundary lines before assuming a well isn't paying you.

Closer to Commerce City and the South Platte corridor, the geology is the same but the surface is more built up — refineries, rail, and dense residential subdivisions. Operators still hold leases here, but new permitting has slowed as local governments and the state's Energy and Carbon Management Commission apply tighter scrutiny to pads near homes and schools.

sections.title: Setback rules changed what's developable
sections.html:
Colorado's 2019 overhaul of oil and gas oversight (SB 19-181) shifted the mission of the state regulator from promoting development to protecting public health and safety, and it opened the door for counties and municipalities to layer on their own surface-use and setback rules. Adams County and its cities have used that authority. The practical effect for a mineral owner is that a tract that looked drillable under the old rules may now sit inside a buffer zone that keeps a pad off the surface entirely, even if the minerals themselves are still perfectly capable of producing through a directional well drilled from outside the buffer.

That distinction — undevelopable surface location versus undevelopable minerals — is one buyers weigh carefully. A tract inside a residential setback zone isn't worthless; it just has to be reached by a longer lateral from a pad sited elsewhere, which changes the timing and the economics but not necessarily the eventual outcome.

sections.title: Split estate and old subdivision severances
sections.html:
A lot of Adams County land was platted for agriculture and ranching long before the suburbs arrived, and mineral rights were commonly severed from the surface in those early transactions — sold, reserved, or willed off separately from the farmland itself. Multiple generations later, a homeowner in a newer Brighton or Commerce City subdivision may have no idea they don't own what's underneath their lot, while a family two counties away holds a fractional mineral interest they've never actively managed.

If you inherited a fractional interest like that, the first useful step isn't calling a buyer — it's pulling the deed history at the Adams County Clerk and Recorder to confirm your exact decimal share and whether the interest has ever been leased. We do this work as part of every offer we make, but knowing your own numbers first puts you in a stronger position either way.

sections.title: What we look at before making an offer
sections.html: For producing interests, we pull twelve to twenty-four months of royalty statements where available and build a decline curve off actual volumes rather than a type-curve assumption. For non-producing interests, we check whether the tract falls inside an existing horizontal unit, whether nearby permits have been filed with the state, and what the local setback map does to surface access. Weld County comparables matter here since Adams shares the same formations, but we adjust for the added regulatory friction on the Adams side of the line.

faqs.q: Does your land need an active well to sell your mineral rights?
faqs.a: No. We buy producing and non-producing interests. Non-producing tracts in the Wattenberg extension zone are priced against nearby permitting activity and decline data from comparable units rather than your own check history, since there isn't one yet.

faqs.q: How do Adams County's local setback rules affect value?
faqs.a: They mostly affect timing and access, not whether minerals exist. A tract inside a residential buffer can still be produced through a longer lateral drilled from a pad sited outside the buffer; that typically pushes out the development timeline, which we build into any offer.

faqs.q: your mineral interest hasn't been leased in years — is it still worth anything?
faqs.a: Often yes, especially if it sits near active Wattenberg units. We check current permitting and unit boundaries around your legal description before quoting, rather than assuming a stale lease means no value.

faqs.q: Where Do you find your ownership documentation?
faqs.a: Start with the Adams County Clerk and Recorder's deed and probate records, which show the chain of title and your decimal mineral interest. We can help pull and interpret that record as part of evaluating your interest.

items.name: Sell Mineral Rights in Arapahoe County, CO
items.meta: Arapahoe County minerals span dense Denver suburbs and open eastern plains. Learn how ownership fragmentation and DJ Basin position affect what your interest is worth.

sections.html:
Ownership fragmentation, not geology, is usually the first problem an Arapahoe County mineral owner has to solve — a single quarter-section reserved a century ago can now trace through a dozen heirs scattered across the country.

Arapahoe County runs from the built-out suburbs of Aurora and Centennial in the west to open dryland farming toward Byers and the Arapahoe-Elbert line in the east. Both ends sit within the broader Denver-Julesburg Basin, but they're at very different points relative to the Wattenberg Field's productive core in Weld County to the north. Western Arapahoe County is mostly residential land where drilling activity is limited by density and local surface-use rules; the eastern county still has working farmland where operators have drilled and, in some cases, are still drilling.

What that means for an owner is that location inside the county matters more here than it does in a place like Weld, where almost everything sits over the same core play. We evaluate Arapahoe County interests parcel by parcel against actual permitting and unit data rather than quoting a flat county-wide number.

sections.title: A history of small severances
sections.html:
A large share of Arapahoe County's original land grants and homestead patents were platted and sold off with the mineral estate severed from the surface — common practice in Colorado agricultural land through the early 20th century. As that farmland was later subdivided into ranchettes, and eventually into suburban tracts around Aurora and Centennial, the severed mineral interests kept passing down through wills and intestate succession, splitting further with each generation.

The result is that many current Arapahoe County mineral owners hold a fractional decimal interest — sometimes a very small one — in a tract they've never seen, alongside cousins or distant relatives they may not know. Sorting out exactly what you own, and whether it's even been leased, usually starts with the probate and deed records at the county clerk and recorder's office rather than with a phone call to a buyer.

sections.title: Western county: suburban density limits new drilling
sections.html: Around Aurora, Centennial, Cherry Hills Village, and the string of small municipalities along the C-470 corridor, the surface is largely built out with housing, retail, and infrastructure. New horizontal development is possible in principle — Colorado operators have drilled directional wells from pads set well outside residential zones to reach minerals under subdivisions — but it's slower, more expensive, and more heavily scrutinized under the setback and local-control rules that followed SB 19-181. A mineral interest here is more likely to be non-producing, or produced by an old vertical well drilled decades before the current density existed.

sections.title: Eastern county: closer to active DJ Basin acreage
sections.html: East of E-470, toward Byers, Bennett, and the Elbert County line, Arapahoe County still has agricultural land where operators have leased and, in pockets, drilled. This ground sits on the southern flank of the DJ Basin rather than in the Wattenberg core, so wells here tend to be shallower producers with different decline behavior than a Weld County Niobrara horizontal — often longer, flatter production histories rather than a steep early decline. If your interest is in this part of the county, recent royalty statements (where you have them) are the single best input for pricing your interest accurately.

sections.title: How we evaluate a fragmented interest
sections.html: For a fractional interest inherited through multiple generations, we start by confirming your decimal share against the deed and probate chain rather than taking a family estimate at face value — that number drives everything else. From there we check whether the tract is inside an active or historical unit, what the operator of record has filed with the state, and, if there's production, what the decline curve looks like against recent volumes. We can typically give a preliminary range before you've assembled a complete title history, then firm it up once documentation is confirmed.

sections.title: Comparing decline behavior across the county
sections.html:
A Weld County horizontal Niobrara well typically shows a steep production decline in its first eighteen months before flattening into a long, low-volume tail. Older vertical wells common in eastern Arapahoe County behave differently — a gentler initial decline, lower peak volumes, but a longer flat stretch that can keep paying modest royalties for years. That difference matters when you're comparing a check history from your own interest to what you might have heard a neighbor's Weld County minerals are producing; the two aren't directly comparable even though both sit in the same basin.

For an heir who inherited a small interest without any operating history to reference, we look at the specific well or unit's public production data filed with the state rather than basin-wide averages, since averages can mislead in either direction depending on well age and completion type.

faqs.q: you only own a small fractional interest — is it worth selling?
faqs.a: Often yes, particularly if the tract sits in an active or historical DJ Basin unit. Small fractional interests are common in Arapahoe County because of decades of inheritance splitting, and we regularly buy interests down to very small decimal shares.

items.name: Sell Mineral Rights in Broomfield County, CO
items.meta: Broomfield's setback fights reshaped DJ Basin drilling near the surface. See how that regulatory history factors into what your mineral or royalty interest is worth.

sections.html:
Broomfield is a combined city and county sitting squarely in the Wattenberg Field's productive footprint, and it's also where some of the most consequential local pushback on urban oil and gas development in Colorado played out.

When operators proposed large multi-well pads near residential neighborhoods in Broomfield in the mid-2010s, the resulting fight — over air monitoring, setback distances, and local authority to say no — became a reference point statewide and helped shape the 2019 legislative overhaul (SB 19-181) that gave Colorado counties and municipalities explicit authority over surface-use rules. Broomfield voters and the city council have since adopted some of the state's more restrictive local setback and monitoring requirements.

For a mineral owner, that history isn't background noise — it directly shapes what's drillable, on what timeline, and under what conditions. We price Broomfield interests against the current local rules and existing unit boundaries, not against what a lease might have promised before those rules tightened.

sections.title: Core Wattenberg geology, uncommonly tight surface rules
sections.html:
Broomfield sits over the same Niobrara-Codell stack that makes Weld County's Wattenberg Field the most productive oil and gas play in Colorado. The rock quality here is genuinely good. What's different is the surface: Broomfield is one of the most densely built residential communities anywhere near active DJ Basin acreage, and the city-county government has used its post-2019 authority to require larger setbacks, additional air and noise monitoring, and more restrictive permitting conditions than many neighboring counties.

That combination — strong subsurface geology, tight surface constraints — means existing pads and units in Broomfield tend to be worked hard once permitted (long laterals, multi-well configurations to minimize surface footprint), while new pad siting has slowed considerably compared to the mid-2010s pace.

sections.title: Forced pooling changes reduced leverage for absent owners
sections.html: Colorado tightened its forced pooling statute in 2023 (SB 23-198), raising the bar operators must clear before including a non-consenting mineral owner's interest in a drilling unit without a negotiated lease. In a densely fragmented ownership environment like Broomfield's residential subdivisions — where a single unit can pull in mineral interests under dozens of separately owned lots — that change affects how quickly and on what terms an operator can bring every owner into a unit. If you own minerals under a Broomfield subdivision and have never been contacted about a lease, that's not unusual; it may reflect the operator working through a longer consent process than it once needed to.

sections.title: What the clerk and recorder's file usually shows
sections.html:
Because Broomfield's residential development largely postdates the original agricultural platting, most mineral severances here trace back to farm and ranch deeds from well before the city-county's incorporation. Pulling that chain at the Broomfield Clerk and Recorder typically turns up the original reservation language, any subsequent lease filings, and whether the interest has been assigned or subdivided among heirs since. That paperwork is the foundation for confirming your exact decimal interest before any offer is finalized.

If your family has held the interest for multiple generations without actively managing it, it's common to find the original lease has expired or been held by production on only part of the unit, which is worth clarifying before assuming either that the interest is dormant or that it's still fully committed to an operator.

sections.title: What determines value here

If it's inside a permitted-but-undrilled area, we look at the operator's public filings and permitting timeline with the state's Energy and Carbon Management Commission. If it sits outside any current unit boundary, we weigh how likely future development is given both the geology and Broomfield's specific local rules, which are stricter than most surrounding jurisdictions.

faqs.q: Why haven't you been offered a lease if your mineral rights are in an active area?
faqs.a: Colorado's 2023 changes to forced pooling raised the requirements operators must meet before pulling non-consenting owners into a unit, which can slow the process in densely subdivided residential areas like much of Broomfield.

faqs.q: How does Broomfield compare to Weld County for mineral value?
faqs.a: The underlying Niobrara-Codell rock is comparable since both sit in the Wattenberg footprint, but Broomfield's tighter local permitting rules generally mean a slower development timeline, which we account for in any offer.

Modern horizontal drilling has made isolated appearances on the eastern plains as operators test whether the economics work at this depth and rock quality, but the pace has never matched the DJ Basin core.

That history shapes how we value interests here. A Cheyenne County mineral tract is far more likely to be evaluated on a long, low-decline stripper-well production history than on a steep new-horizontal-well curve, and the ownership behind it is often tangled up in generations of dryland wheat-farming families and old homestead patents.

sections.title: Stripper wells behave differently than horizontal Wattenberg wells
sections.html:
A horizontal Niobrara well in Weld County typically produces most of its lifetime volume in the first two to three years, then declines sharply. A conventional vertical well of the kind common in Cheyenne County does the opposite — modest peak production early, followed by decades of low, comparatively stable output. That's the definition of a stripper well, and Colorado has plenty of them out on the eastern plains, some still owned and operated by small independent producers rather than the larger companies active in the DJ core.

If you're comparing what you've heard about Weld County mineral sales to your own Cheyenne County royalty checks, the numbers won't look alike, and that's expected — the well type and decline profile are fundamentally different, not a sign that your interest is being shortchanged.

sections.title: Checkerboard ownership from homestead-era patents
sections.html:
Much of Cheyenne County's land was settled under federal homestead and railroad land-grant programs in the late 1800s and early 1900s, which produced a genuinely checkerboarded pattern of surface and mineral ownership across the county — alternating sections owned by different original patentees, some of whom severed minerals at the time of sale and some who didn't. Combined with a century of farm-family inheritance since, a single quarter-section can now carry mineral ownership split among a dozen or more heirs, several of whom may have moved away from Colorado entirely and lost track of what they own.

We regularly work with owners in this position who are starting from limited information — a mention of the interest in a will, or a small royalty check from decades ago with no other paperwork attached. Confirming the interest through the Cheyenne County Clerk and Recorder's deed and probate records is usually the first real step, and we can help with that research directly.

items.name: Sell Mineral Rights in Larimer County, CO

sections.html:
Larimer County straddles the transition zone where the DJ Basin's Niobrara and Codell benches thin out against the Front Range foothills, producing a patchwork of active wells, undrilled acreage, and heavily regulated setback zones.

Larimer County runs from the dense Fort Collins and Loveland corridor out to mountain communities like Red Feather Lakes, and mineral ownership here reflects that range. Sections east of you-25 near Loveland sit close enough to the Wattenberg core to have seen real horizontal development; sections further west and north are largely undrilled ranch and foothill ground where minerals have sat quiet for generations.

If you inherited a mineral interest somewhere in Larimer County and don't know which category it falls into, that's the first thing we sort out — because the difference between an actively producing DJ Basin interest and undeveloped flank acreage changes the valuation by an order of magnitude.

sections.title: Local control and setback rules matter more here than in Weld County
sections.html:
Colorado's 2019 legislation, SB 19-181, shifted oil and gas regulatory authority toward local governments and made public health and safety the top priority in permitting decisions. Larimer County and its municipalities have used that authority to adopt setback and review standards that are, in places, more restrictive than the state's baseline rules — which has slowed new permitting in populated areas even where the geology would otherwise support development.

That regulatory layer is a real part of the valuation conversation for Larimer County acreage. An interest near an existing, grandfathered well faces a very different development outlook than an undrilled tract in an area now covered by tighter local setbacks, and we factor that in rather than pricing every parcel the same.

sections.title: Where the active production actually sits
sections.html:
The productive core of Larimer County's DJ Basin acreage runs along the county's southeastern edge, blending into the Wattenberg field footprint that dominates Weld County next door. Wells here target the same Niobrara B and C benches and Codell sandstone as their Weld County counterparts, drilled on comparable spacing units and showing the same steep-early, long-tail decline pattern.

Further north and west, toward Laporte and the foothills, drilling has always been sparser, both because of thinning formation economics and because that ground sits closer to residential and recreational land uses that draw more regulatory scrutiny.

items.name: Sell Mineral Rights in Yuma County, CO
items.meta: Yuma County sits on the DJ Basin's eastern plains margin, with homestead-era ownership and legacy vertical wells. Get a comp-based cash offer today.

sections.html:
Yuma County is the DJ Basin's quieter eastern edge, dryland farm ground where legacy vertical production and homestead-era ownership shape almost every transaction we work here.

Yuma County sits at the far eastern reach of Colorado's D-J Basin, where the Niobrara and Codell formations run shallower and generally less prolific than they do in the deep Wattenberg core two hours west in Weld County. This is dryland wheat, corn, and cattle country, and it's been that way since homesteaders claimed the land under federal patents in the early 20th century, decades before anyone drilled the first well here.

Because the geology and the development history are genuinely different from the DJ Basin's core, we treat Yuma County as its own market rather than pricing it off Weld County comps. What follows is how we actually think about a Yuma County mineral interest.

sections.title: Eastern margin geology and well economics
sections.html:
The Niobrara chalk and underlying Codell sandstone extend across much of Yuma County, but reservoir quality and thickness generally decline moving east away from the Wattenberg core, and well results here are more variable section to section than in central Weld County. That variability is exactly why we look at nearby producing wells and any recent horizontal test activity in your specific township before quoting a number, rather than applying a flat countywide figure.

A meaningful share of Yuma County's historical production also comes from older vertical wells drilled well before the current horizontal drilling era, some going back decades. These wells have settled into long, low-volume decline curves, essentially stripper production, which is a different kind of asset to value than a newly completed horizontal well but not a lesser one; a mature well's long production history actually gives us a more reliable curve to price against.

sections.title: What the Wray courthouse tells us
sections.html: Every Yuma County offer starts with the record. We pull your deed history through the county Clerk and Recorder, verify the mineral reservation survived every subsequent transfer of the surface, cross-check any existing division order or lease, and confirm whether your tract sits inside a current or historical spacing unit before landing on a price. Yuma County land records run further back than most Front Range counties in continuous single-family ownership, which can actually make the chain easier to trace once we're past the original patent.

sections.title: Rural surface, fewer local siting disputes
sections.html: Unlike the Front Range suburbs where SB 19-181 triggered years of local setback fights between operators and residential neighborhoods, Yuma County's surface remains almost entirely agricultural. That means operators here generally don't face the same local permitting friction seen in places like Adams or Broomfield County, which tends to make development timelines more predictable once a well is economically justified, even if overall drilling pace is slower than in the Wattenberg core.

sections.title: Homestead-era ownership and fractionalized heirs
sections.html:
Nearly all of Yuma County's private land was originally claimed under the Homestead Act or similar federal land patents, section by section, in the decades around 1900. Mineral interests today routinely trace back to those original patents, and after four or five generations of inheritance it's common to find a single quarter section's mineral estate split among a dozen or more living heirs, each holding a small fractional percentage.

That inheritance pattern is the single biggest complicating factor in a Yuma County transaction. Before we quote anything, we build the chain of title back through as many transfers as it takes, using the Yuma County Clerk and Recorder's office in Wray, to confirm exactly what percentage you personally hold today. It's common for a fractional owner to have no idea their family still held anything until a landman or a title search surfaces it.

faqs.q: Why is Yuma County priced differently than Weld County?
faqs.a: The Niobrara and Codell run shallower and less consistently productive toward the eastern plains, so well economics and royalty value here are generally lower than in the deep Wattenberg core. We price against eastern-margin comps specific to Yuma County.

faqs.q: A Colorado mineral-owning family has owned this mineral interest since the original homestead. How do you confirm your share?
faqs.a: We trace the chain of title through the Yuma County Clerk and Recorder in Wray back to the original land patent, confirming every transfer and inheritance along the way to establish your exact fractional interest.

faqs.q: Is a legacy stripper well interest still worth selling?
faqs.a: Yes. A mature, low-volume well has a long, well-documented decline curve, which lets us price it with real confidence even though the monthly volumes are modest.

faqs.q: Does Yuma County face the same local drilling restrictions as Front Range suburbs?
faqs.a: Generally not to the same degree. The surface here remains largely agricultural, so operators face fewer local setback disputes than in residential Front Range counties, though overall drilling pace still depends on commodity pricing.

faqs.q: How long does closing take on a Yuma County interest?
faqs.a: Once we've confirmed your chain of title through the county record, most Yuma County transactions close within three to four weeks, sometimes longer if the heir chain is complex.

items.name: Inherited Mineral Rights
items.meta: Inherited Colorado mineral rights and unsure what they're worth or whether to keep them? We walk heirs through valuation, title, and a clean sale option.

sections.html:
Inheriting a Colorado mineral interest usually comes with more questions than the estate paperwork answers, starting with what it's actually worth and whether keeping it makes sense.

Heirs to Colorado mineral rights, especially interests tracing back to a grandparent's or great-grandparent's homestead in Weld, Garfield, or La Plata County, often inherit an asset they know almost nothing about: no clear sense of how many acres, which formation, whether the interest is leased, or what a royalty check history actually looks like. Sometimes the first sign of ownership is a division order letter or a check arriving out of nowhere after an estate closes.

We help heirs sort out exactly what they hold, whether it's producing, non-producing, or leased-but-undrilled, and give a straight valuation so the decision to keep or sell is based on real numbers rather than a guess.

sections.title: Figuring out what you actually inherited
sections.html:
The first step is usually confirming the interest is legally in your name. If the estate went through probate, there should be a deed or court order transferring the mineral interest to you; if it didn't, or if the property was informally passed down for a generation or two, that chain needs to be cleared up before a sale, and sometimes even before you can collect royalty payments the operator is currently holding in suspense.

Once title is confirmed, we pull the recorded lease, county production records, and any available division order history to build a full picture: whether wells are currently producing on the tract, which formation they target, and how the interest has performed over recent years.

sections.title: Keep, lease, or sell
sections.html:
Keeping an inherited interest makes sense for some heirs, particularly if the royalty stream is meaningful and stable, or if there's sentimental value in holding onto family land ties. But many heirs end up with a small, split, or non-producing interest that's more administrative burden than income, especially when it's shared with siblings or cousins who each want something different done with it.

Selling converts an uncertain, sometimes hard-to-value future royalty stream into a known amount today, and it eliminates the ongoing paperwork, tax reporting, and division order corrections that come with an inherited interest, particularly one you didn't ask for and don't have the records to manage confidently.

sections.title: Basis, taxes, and what to ask your CPA
sections.html:
Inherited mineral rights generally receive a stepped-up basis to fair market value as of the date of death, which is different from what the original owner paid or was leased for decades ago. That basis matters directly for any future sale, since it's what capital gain or loss is measured against. Talk to your CPA or tax advisor about how basis and any prior depletion apply to your specific situation before you sell.

We can provide documentation of the sale price and date to support your tax reporting, but we're a mineral buyer, not a tax professional, so the specifics of your return should go through your own advisor.

sections.title: When siblings inherit together and disagree
sections.html:
It's common for a mineral interest to pass to multiple siblings or cousins jointly, and just as common for them to disagree about what to do with it: one wants to hold for the income, another wants to sell and move on. Each heir generally has the right to sell their own undivided share independently, regardless of what the others decide, so disagreement among co-heirs doesn't have to stall the whole family's options.

We can work with heirs individually on their own timeline, or coordinate a single closing if the family prefers to sell together, and we're comfortable explaining the process separately to each sibling if that makes the conversation easier.

faqs.q: How do you know if your inherited mineral rights are producing?
faqs.a: We check county production records and, if available, division order history tied to your tract. If there's active production nearby but you've never received a check, the operator may be holding payments in suspense pending title confirmation.

faqs.q: Do you need to go through probate before you can sell?
faqs.a: If the interest wasn't formally transferred to you through probate or an affidavit of heirship, that typically needs to happen first. We can explain what's required for your specific estate.

faqs.q: What's your inherited interest worth compared to what your relative paid?
faqs.a: Inherited minerals generally get a stepped-up basis to fair market value at the date of death, unrelated to the original purchase or lease price decades ago. Ask your CPA how that applies to your sale.

faqs.q: Should you keep it, lease it, or sell it?
faqs.a: It depends on the size of the interest, whether it's producing, and how much administrative burden you're willing to carry, especially if it's shared with siblings. We'll give you a clear valuation either way so the decision is based on real numbers.

faqs.q: The check is in your deceased relative's name. What Do you do?
faqs.a: Contact the operator's division order desk to begin the transfer process and confirm what documentation, typically a death certificate and probate or heirship paperwork, they require before reissuing checks in your name.

items.name: Got an Unsolicited Offer?
items.meta: Received an unsolicited offer for your Colorado mineral rights? We'll run the same decline-curve math independently so you know if it's fair before you sign.

sections.html:
A letter showed up offering to buy your Colorado minerals, and now the question is whether that number reflects real analysis or just a low anchor hoping you don't check.

Unsolicited mailbox offers for Colorado mineral rights are common, especially in active areas like Weld County, where several buyers send blanket letters to every owner of record in a county without necessarily reviewing individual production history first. Some of these offers are reasonable starting points; others are set deliberately low, betting that an owner without a comparison won't know the difference.

We'll run the same underwriting on your interest, pulling division order check history or offset activity depending on whether you're producing or not, and give you an independent number to compare against what you received. There's no obligation to sell to us; sometimes the honest answer is that the offer you already have is fair.

sections.title: What a real analysis looks like versus a blanket letter
sections.html:
A genuine valuation starts with your actual production or lease history, not a flat per-acre number applied across an entire county regardless of which formation, bench, or spacing unit your specific tract sits in. Blanket mailers are often priced off general county activity rather than your well's actual decline curve, which is why two neighbors with different well vintages can receive suspiciously similar offers.

When you send us your check stubs or lease documents, we build a number specific to your interest: recent decline behavior, offset activity, and where your interest sits relative to core versus flank development. That's a different process than a form letter, and it usually produces a different number.

sections.title: Questions worth asking before you sign anything
sections.html:
Ask the buyer how they arrived at the number specifically for your tract, not only for the general area. Ask whether the offer accounts for your actual decline curve or a generic assumption. And check the deed language carefully; some offers are structured to acquire more than you intend to sell, such as all depths rather than just the currently producing formation, or a term longer than expected.

We're glad to review a deed or purchase agreement you've already received and flag anything worth asking the other buyer about, even if you end up selling to them and not to us.

sections.title: No pressure, no deadline games
sections.html: Some unsolicited offers come with an artificial deadline, sign by a certain date or the offer expires, which is a pressure tactic more than a reflection of real market timing. Mineral value doesn't typically change meaningfully in a two-week window barring major news on your specific well. Take the time to get a second number before signing anything.

sections.title: Why offers on the same street can differ
sections.html:
It's not unusual for two neighbors receiving mailbox offers to see different numbers, even on tracts that look similar from the road, because their underlying interests often aren't actually alike: different decimal fractions, different well vintages within the same spacing unit, or one interest tied to a bench that's further into decline than the other. A lower offer to one neighbor doesn't necessarily mean the buyer is treating that owner unfairly.

That's exactly why we recommend building your own comparison from your specific check history rather than comparing notes with a neighbor and assuming the numbers should match. We're happy to walk through the differences with you if you want to understand why two interests priced differently.

faqs.q: Is it normal to get an unsolicited offer for mineral rights?
faqs.a: Yes, particularly if you own minerals in an active area like Weld County. Multiple buyers send letters based on county ownership records without necessarily reviewing your specific production history first.

faqs.q: How do you know if the offer you received is fair?
faqs.a: Send us your check stubs or lease documents and we'll run our own independent valuation based on your actual decline curve or offset activity, so you have a real comparison rather than guessing.

faqs.q: The offer has a deadline to sign. Should you feel pressured?
faqs.a: Generally no. Mineral value doesn't shift meaningfully in a two-week window absent major news specific to your well. A deadline is usually a pressure tactic, not a reflection of real timing.

faqs.q: Is it worth getting a second opinion even if the first offer seems reasonable?
faqs.a: Usually yes, since it costs you nothing to compare. Even a fair-seeming offer can leave value on the table if it wasn't built from your specific check history, and a second number confirms whether that's the case.

faqs.q: The deed they sent you looks complicated. What Should you look for?
faqs.a: Check what depths and formations are actually being conveyed, not only the producing zone, and confirm the term matches what you expect. We can review a deed you've already received and flag anything worth questioning.

faqs.q: If your number is higher, will you match or beat the letter you already have?
faqs.a: We'll give you our honest independent number based on your actual production and offset activity. If it's higher, that's simply what our underwriting supports, not a bidding tactic against the other offer.

items.name: Out-of-State Owners
items.meta: Live outside Colorado but own minerals in Weld, Garfield, or La Plata County? We handle the full sale remotely, by mail and phone, no trip required.

sections.html:
You don't need to fly to Colorado, visit a courthouse, or track down a local notary in a county you've never set foot in. We handle all of it remotely.

A large share of Colorado mineral owners live nowhere near the acreage they own, having inherited an interest from a relative who homesteaded or ranched in Weld, Garfield, or La Plata County generations ago while the family scattered elsewhere. Managing that interest from out of state, tracking division order corrections, deciphering an unfamiliar check stub, figuring out who to call when a letter arrives, is its own kind of burden, separate from whatever the interest is actually worth.

We work with out-of-state owners constantly and run the entire transaction remotely: title review pulled from county records without you needing to visit, documents sent by mail or secure electronic delivery, and closing handled through a title company or attorney without requiring you to be in Colorado at any point.

sections.title: What we handle so you don't have to travel
sections.html:
Title and chain-of-ownership research happens at the county clerk and recorder's office, which we pull directly rather than asking you to track down documents. If your interest was inherited and never formally retitled, we'll walk you through what's needed, often an affidavit of heirship or probate documentation, that can typically be handled through your local courthouse or a notary near you, not one in Colorado.

Once we've confirmed the interest and agreed on a number, closing documents are sent to you directly. Most owners sign with a local notary near their home and return everything by mail or overnight courier; we don't require an in-person closing in Colorado.

sections.title: Confirming value without seeing the land
sections.html:
You don't need to have ever visited the acreage for us to value it fairly. We work from your division order or check stub history for producing interests, and from county production and permit records for non-producing or leased-but-undrilled tracts, the same data we'd use whether you lived next door to the well or across the country from it.

If you're unsure exactly what county your interest sits in, or your paperwork is old and references a homestead or family ranch by name rather than a legal description, send what you have. We can usually trace it through the county records ourselves.

sections.title: Mail forwarding and lost checks
sections.html:
Operators send division order checks and correspondence to whatever address is on file, and that address can go stale for years if an out-of-state owner moves without notifying every operator paying them. If you've had checks go missing or held in suspense, we can help identify which operator needs an updated address as part of our title review, since resolving that is often a prerequisite to closing a clean sale.

This is a common issue for owners who inherited an interest from a relative who lived in Colorado decades ago; the mailing address on file may still reflect an address that no longer exists.

sections.title: Tax and reporting across state lines
sections.html: Colorado mineral income and any sale proceeds may have state tax implications even though you live elsewhere, and Colorado generally requires nonresident withholding on real property sales, which mineral interests fall under. We can provide the closing documentation your CPA needs, but the specifics of your filing should go through your own tax advisor, since it depends on your home state's rules too.

sections.title: Communication that doesn't require a Colorado phone number
sections.html:
Being out of state shouldn't mean being out of the loop on your own transaction. We keep out-of-state owners updated by phone and email at each stage, title confirmation, valuation, and document delivery, so there's no need to guess at status or wonder whether a piece of mail got lost somewhere between Colorado and wherever you're living now.

If you'd rather have your own attorney or a family member local to Colorado review documents on your behalf before you sign, we're glad to work with them directly alongside you.

faqs.q: Do you need to travel to Colorado to sell your mineral rights?
faqs.a: No. We handle title research, document delivery, and closing remotely. Most out-of-state owners sign with a notary near their own home and return paperwork by mail.

faqs.q: you have never seen the land and don't know exactly where it is. Can you still help?
faqs.a: Yes. Send whatever paperwork you have, even an old deed referencing a family homestead by name, and we can usually trace it through the relevant county's records.

faqs.q: Will you owe Colorado state tax on the sale even though you live elsewhere?
faqs.a: Possibly. Colorado generally applies nonresident withholding to real property sales, which includes minerals. Talk to your CPA about how that applies to your specific situation.

faqs.q: How do you know the interest you're quoting is actually your mineral interest?
faqs.a: We confirm your chain of title directly through the county clerk and recorder's records before closing, independent of anything you send us, so the interest is verified on our end too.

items.name: Minerals in Probate & Estates
items.meta: Executor handling Colorado mineral rights in an estate? We work with probate timelines, court approval requirements, and multi-heir estates to close cleanly.

sections.html:
As executor, you're on the clock and on the hook for getting estate assets valued and settled correctly, and mineral rights are usually the asset nobody in the family knows how to handle.

Executors and personal representatives handling a Colorado estate frequently run into mineral or royalty interests that the deceased owned for decades without much documentation, sometimes tracing back to a Weld County homestead or a Garfield County ranch purchased generations ago. Part of the executor's job is getting these interests properly valued for the estate inventory and, often, deciding whether to distribute them to heirs in kind or liquidate them as part of settling the estate.

We work directly with executors, estate attorneys, and probate courts to value Colorado mineral interests accurately and, where a sale makes sense for the estate, close it within the timeline probate requires.

sections.title: Valuation for the estate inventory
sections.html:
Colorado probate generally requires a fair market valuation of estate assets, including mineral interests, often as of the date of death for basis purposes. For a producing interest we build that valuation from division order check history; for non-producing or leased acreage we look at offset drilling activity and lease terms in the county. We provide documentation of how we reached the number, which typically satisfies what the estate's attorney or the court needs on file.

This valuation matters beyond the sale itself. It sets the stepped-up basis heirs will use if they eventually sell the interest later, so getting it right at this stage has real downstream tax consequences worth getting correct the first time.

sections.title: Court approval and executor authority
sections.html:
Whether you need court approval to sell an estate's mineral interest depends on the authority granted in the will, the type of probate administration opened, and whether all heirs consent to the sale. Some Colorado estates proceed under informal administration where the personal representative has broad authority to sell assets without a separate court hearing; others require formal approval. Your estate attorney can confirm which applies, and we're glad to provide whatever documentation the court process requires on our end.

If multiple heirs each inherit a fractional share rather than the estate selling as a whole, we can work with each heir individually once their interest is formally distributed, or coordinate a single sale that closes the interest before distribution, whichever the estate's attorney recommends.

sections.title: Working around probate timelines
sections.html: Probate has its own schedule, creditor claim periods, inventory deadlines, final accounting, and mineral interests sometimes need to be resolved by a specific point in that process. We move efficiently on title review and closing once the estate is ready to sell, so the mineral asset doesn't become the item holding up the rest of the estate's settlement.

sections.title: When the estate holds several small interests
sections.html:
It's common for an estate to include several small mineral interests scattered across different counties or even different states, accumulated by the deceased over decades without much organization. Rather than valuing and closing each one as a separate transaction, we can often review the full list together and coordinate a combined process, which is usually faster and less burdensome for an executor already managing the rest of the estate's inventory and deadlines.
